title: Interfaces in Depth
description: Interface declarations, multiple interface implementation, default methods, and functional interfaces.
objectives: Declare and implement interfaces thoroughly, including multiple interfaces
Use default methods to evolve an interface without breaking implementers
Understand what makes an interface a functional interface

content.heading: Multiple Interfaces and Default Methods
content.body:
A single class can implement multiple interfaces, separated by commas: class Duck implements Swimmable, Flyable { ... } — this is how Java achieves a form of multiple inheritance of behavior/contract without the ambiguity of multiple class inheritance, since interfaces (mostly) only specify what must be done, not shared mutable state. If two implemented interfaces both declare a default method with the same signature, the implementing class must explicitly override it to resolve the conflict, or the code fails to compile — Java forces this ambiguity to be resolved explicitly rather than picking one arbitrarily.

Default methods exist largely to let library authors add new methods to an existing, widely-implemented interface without breaking every class that already implements it — a class that doesn't override the new default method simply inherits the interface's provided implementation instead of failing to compile.

content.heading: Functional Interfaces
content.body: A functional interface is one with exactly one abstract method (it may still have default and static methods) — this single-abstract-method shape is exactly what allows a lambda expression to implement it concisely, since the lambda's body directly supplies that one method's implementation. The @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but documents intent and causes a compile error if the interface accidentally gains a second abstract method. java.util.function provides many ready-made functional interfaces (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier — covered further in the Lambda Expressions lesson) so you rarely need to declare your own for common shapes.

content.explanation: Duck implements two unrelated interfaces at once. Calculator's single abstract method makes it a valid target for the lambda (a, b) -> a + b, which supplies calculate()'s implementation directly.

keyPoints: A class can implement multiple interfaces, separated by commas
Default methods let an interface evolve without breaking existing implementers
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, making it a valid lambda target
@FunctionalInterface documents intent and enforces the single-abstract-method rule at compile time
commonMistakes: Adding a second abstract method to what was meant to be a functional interface, silently breaking lambda usages
Not resolving a default-method conflict when implementing two interfaces that both provide one with the same signature
Confusing an interface's default methods with an abstract class's regular concrete methods (interfaces still can't hold instance state)
